html:
Russian and Soviet rule in Central Asia lasted from the fall of Tashkent in 1865 to the break-up of the Soviet Union in 1991. In those years Russia and then the USSR ruled the oases and steppes from the Caspian to China.

The Russian Empire had already absorbed the Kazakh steppe. Then it moved south:

  • 1865: Russia took Tashkent. In 1867 it became the seat of the Governorate-General of Turkestan.
  • 1868 and 1873: Bukhara and Khiva became protectorates; the Uzbek khanates kept their rulers but lost their independence.
  • 1876: Kokand was annexed.
  • 1881 to 1885: the Turkmen were conquered.

Russia ran the region much like a colony. It built railways and turned the oases toward cotton for Russian mills. Russian settlers took land on the steppe. In 1916 an order to draft Central Asians for labour behind the front set off a large revolt, crushed with heavy loss of life.

After the Russian Revolution, the Bolsheviks took control, against long resistance from the Basmachi rebels. In 1924 the Soviet republics were drawn, creating the borders of today's five states.

Soviet rule brought schools, literacy, women out of the veil, and industry. It also brought:

  • the Kazakh famine of 1930 to 1933, caused by collectivisation
  • Stalin's purges and the deportation of whole peoples to the region
  • cotton irrigation that made the Aral Sea shrink
  • the space launch site at Baikonur and nuclear tests near Semipalatinsk

It ended when the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991 and the independent republics were born.
sum: Russian and Soviet rule in Central Asia lasted from the fall of Tashkent in 1865 to the break-up of the Soviet Union in 1991. In those years Russia and then the USSR ruled the oases and steppes from the Caspian to China.
